bt800-rfa-798.title: Annales regni Francorum, ed. Friedrich Kurze (MGH Scriptores rerum Germanicarum 6, Hannover 1895)
bt800-rfa-798.institution: Internet Archive, scan of the 1895 edition (University of Toronto copy)
bt800-rfa-798.locator: s.a. 798, pp. 102–105, with Kurze's note 4 on p. 105
bt800-rfa-798.scopedClaim: The Nordliudi living beyond the Elbe seized and killed royal legates at Easter 798; Thrasco, dux of the Obodrites, the Franks' allies, defeated them at Suentana, which Kurze's note identifies with Bornhöved.
bt800-rfa-798.uncertainty: The annal names the Obodrites' leader dux and the battle site, not the borders of either people.
bt800-rfa-798.license: Reference only; no source prose or images redistributed

bt800-rfa-789.title: Annales regni Francorum, ed. Friedrich Kurze (MGH Scriptores rerum Germanicarum 6, Hannover 1895)
bt800-rfa-789.institution: Internet Archive, scan of the 1895 edition (University of Toronto copy)
bt800-rfa-789.locator: s.a. 789, pp. 84–85 and 87, with Kurze's notes 2–3 on p. 84
bt800-rfa-789.scopedClaim: The Wilzi (Welatabi) were a Slavic people on the Baltic coast, hostile to the Franks; Charles crossed the Elbe into their land, a Frisian fleet came up the Havel, and Dragawit ranked first among the other Wilzi reguli. Kurze's note says the name covered all Slavs between the Obodrites and the Sorbs.
bt800-rfa-789.chronology: The annal's year 789, eleven years before the start.
bt800-rfa-789.uncertainty: The passage gives the Wilzi several reguli and no single ruler; it draws no border.
bt800-rfa-789.license: Reference only; no source prose or images redistributed

bt800-rfa-806.title: Annales regni Francorum, ed. Friedrich Kurze (MGH Scriptores rerum Germanicarum 6, Hannover 1895)
bt800-rfa-806.institution: Internet Archive, scan of the 1895 edition (University of Toronto copy)
bt800-rfa-806.scopedClaim: Charles the Younger led an army against the Slavs called Sorbs, who sit on the Elbe; Miliduoch, a dux of the Slavs, was killed and two forts were built, one on the Saale and one by the Elbe.

bt800-kb-isawa.title: Kuwabara Shigeo, 胆沢城 (Isawa castle), 改訂新版 世界大百科事典
bt800-kb-isawa.locator: Entry "胆沢城", section 改訂新版 世界大百科事典, first two paragraphs
bt800-kb-isawa.scopedClaim: Campaigns against the Emishi of the Isawa land, the Kitakami river basin in southern Iwate, were repeated through the Hōki and Enryaku eras; in 801 Sakanoue no Tamuramaro is said to have suppressed their long revolt, and Isawa castle was built in 803 in the former city of Mizusawa.
bt800-kb-isawa.uncertainty: Other dictionaries on the same page date the castle to 802 and name Aterui as one Emishi leader, without saying he ruled all Emishi; the entry names no single Emishi ruler.
bt800-kb-isawa.license: Reference only; no source prose or images redistributed

tribes.noteEn: The annal calls Thrasco dux of the Obodrites, Frankish allies; the point is Wismar, 7 km from the Obodrite trading site.

The point is Brandenburg on the Havel, chosen from the Frisian route up the Havel and Kurze's note placing the Wilzi between the Obodrites and the Sorbs; no source names the town. The revised annal puts the Wilzi on the Baltic coast, north of this point.
The point is Leipzig, between the Elbe and the Saale.
The annal names their dux, Lecho, in 805.
The annal calls them Nordliudi beyond the Elbe; royal legates were holding court among them when they rose in 798. The point is Bornhöved, the battle site.
The Breton duces surrendered to a Frankish count in 799; the revised annal says the conquest did not last.
The point is Mizusawa in the Isawa land; by the entry's account the court suppressed the Isawa Emishi in 801.

bt1200-loc-estonia.title: Estonia: History, Early History
bt1200-loc-estonia.institution: U.S. Library of Congress, Federal Research Division, Country Studies; countrystudies.us copy
bt1200-loc-estonia.scopedClaim: Before 1200 the Estonians lived largely as free peasants loosely organized into parishes, which were grouped into counties; their resistance to the German crusaders lasted some twenty years and failed in 1227, in part for lack of a centralized political organization.
bt1200-loc-estonia.uncertainty: The study names no county, parish or elder before 1227; it names towns (Tallinn, Tartu) only for the conquest and Hanseatic periods.
bt1200-loc-estonia.license: Reference only; no source prose or images redistributed

bt1200-loc-lithuania.title: Lithuania: History, Early History
bt1200-loc-lithuania.institution: U.S. Library of Congress, Federal Research Division, Country Studies; countrystudies.us copy
bt1200-loc-lithuania.locator: Section "Early History", first and second paragraphs
bt1200-loc-lithuania.scopedClaim: Lithuania emerged as a nation about 1230 under Duke Mindaugas, who united the Lithuanian tribes against the Teutonic Knights; the Knights had conquered the kindred tribes of Prussia.
bt1200-loc-lithuania.chronology: About 1230; the Prussian conquest is undated.
bt1200-loc-lithuania.uncertainty: The study gives no picture of the Lithuanian tribes in 1200 and no date for the Prussian conquest.
bt1200-loc-lithuania.license: Reference only; no source prose or images redistributed

bt1200-lex-preussen.title: Preussen
bt1200-lex-preussen.locator: Fact box and the paragraph on the origin of the name
bt1200-lex-preussen.scopedClaim: The name Prussia comes from the Baltic people of the Prussians, who in the Middle Ages lived between the Vistula and the Neman, spoke Old Prussian, and were subjugated and christianized by the Teutonic Order in the 13th century.
bt1200-lex-preussen.chronology: Middle Ages; conquest in the 13th century.
bt1200-lex-preussen.uncertainty: The article gives no year within the 13th century and says nothing about Prussian leaders before the conquest.

bt1500-braniff.title: Beatriz Braniff Cornejo, Comercio e interrelaciones entre Mesoamérica y la Gran Chichimeca, in Janet Long Towell and Amalia Attolini Lecón (coords.), Caminos y mercados de México (2009), pp. 27–50
bt1500-braniff.institution: Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Instituto de Investigaciones Históricas; Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia
bt1500-braniff.locator: Section "Los territorios", pp. 28–30 with figs. 1–2, including the paragraph naming Altavista, Zacatecas; p. 31, first paragraph (Postclassic nomadism)
bt1500-braniff.scopedClaim: After the first millennium AD the region Braniff calls Mesoamérica Chichimeca, which includes Altavista in Zacatecas, passed to hunter-gatherer groups such as the Guamares, Guachichiles and Zacatecos, whom the Mexica and the Spaniards knew in the 16th century.
bt1500-braniff.uncertainty: Braniff draws the region on a map and gives no year; she says nothing about the groups' leaders.
bt1500-braniff.license: Reference only; no source prose or images redistributed

bt1500-langer-chiriguanos.title: Erick D. Langer, Chiriguanos
bt1500-langer-chiriguanos.institution: Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture (Gale); Encyclopedia.com
bt1500-langer-chiriguanos.locator: Opening sentences (migration, Incas) and the sentence after the 17th-century population estimate (government)
bt1500-langer-chiriguanos.scopedClaim: The Chiriguanos, descendants of the Tupi-Guaraní, migrated in the 15th century to the foothills of the southeastern Bolivian Andes and threatened the Incas, who built fortresses against them; their government was highly decentralized, under village chiefs who accepted the loose leadership of regional chiefs.
bt1500-langer-chiriguanos.chronology: 15th-century migration; the government is described as a lasting feature into the colonial period.
bt1500-langer-chiriguanos.uncertainty: The entry gives no year for the migration and describes the government chiefly for the colonial period.
bt1500-langer-chiriguanos.license: Reference only; no source prose or images redistributed
